Empirical Research Plan: “Valid Inference for Treatment Effects at a Known Cutoff when the Bandwidth Is Large”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) and its three common extensions  
  • Sharp RD (level jump)  
  • Sharp RKD (slope kink)  
  • Fuzzy RD (discrete jump in treatment probability)  
  • Fuzzy RKD (slope kink in treatment probability)  

Why RDD/RKD?  
 • The assignment mechanism is entirely score-based and the cutoff is known ex-ante, so the identifying variation is local to the threshold.  
 • The research question is explicitly about how to conduct inference for the average treatment effect at that point.  
 • DID, IV, or event-study frameworks are unnecessary because no time dimension or separate instrument beyond the score is needed.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Running variable, Xi: continuous score that determines eligibility (e.g., poverty index, vote share, test score).  
Cutoff, c: the known threshold. Without loss of generality, normalise c = 0.  

For each design we define  

A. Sharp RD  
   Ti = 1{Xi ≥ 0}.  
   Treatment group: observations with Xi ≥ 0 (just to the right).  
   Control group: observations with Xi < 0 (just to the left).  

B. Fuzzy RD  
   Zi = 1{Xi ≥ 0} is the assignment indicator (first‐stage jump);  
   Ti is the realised treatment status (partial compliance).  
   Use Zi as an instrument for Ti.  

C. Sharp RKD  
   Ti is a continuous treatment whose marginal schedule kinks at Xi = 0  
   (e.g., marginal tax rate).  
   Identification: slope change in E[Yi | Xi].  

D. Fuzzy RKD  
   Same as C, but kink is in E[Ti | Xi] rather than in Ti itself; use the kink in assignment as an instrument.  

Timing/Event date: Not applicable; cross-sectional design.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity (or differentiability) of potential outcome functions at the cutoff.  
     • In a kink setup, require continuity of first derivative.  
     • Plausible because the threshold is administratively set and agents have limited ability to precisely manipulate Xi.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable (McCrary test yields no discontinuity in density at c).  

A3. For fuzzy designs, monotonicity/compliance: crossing the cutoff does not reduce the probability of treatment for any unit.  

A4. Sufficient information: The conditional variance and higher moments of Yi are well-behaved in a neighbourhood of c, allowing for valid local polynomial approximations.  

Given common administrative scores (poverty index, vote margin), these assumptions are widely regarded as credible, though they must be tested empirically.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Manipulation/Sorting around the cutoff  
  • Conduct McCrary density test.  
  • Examine bunching graphs.  
  • If manipulation is detected, shift design to an RKD or use donut RDD dropping ±h0 window where sorting is evident.  

Threat 2: Misspecification and bias from using a large bandwidth  
  • Employ robust bias-corrected (RBC) confidence intervals à la Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik (2014, 2023).  
  • Complement with the “honest” CI approach that inflates variance to cover worst-case bias for a given h (Armstrong–Kolesár, 2020).  

Threat 3: Heteroskedasticity and clustered outcomes (e.g., Progresa households within villages)  
  • Use heteroskedasticity-robust nearest-neighbour variance estimators.  
  • When grouping exists, cluster at the village or district level.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
install.packages(c("data.table", "rdrobust", "rddensity", "fixest"))
library(data.table); library(rdrobust); library(rddensity); library(fixest)

# ---- 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------
# Assume CSV named 'progresa.csv' with hh_id, village, score, treat, outcome
dt <- fread("progresa.csv")

# ---- 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------
c <- 0                       # cutoff, already centered
dt[, x  := score - c]        # running variable centered
dt[, z  := as.integer(x >= 0)]# assignment indicator (fuzzy designs)
# For sharp designs we set treat = z; for fuzzy we keep actual treat
# Keep a symmetric window of, say, |x| <= 0.5 for descriptive plots
plot_dt <- dt[abs(x) <= 0.5]

# ---- 3. Manipulation test ---------------------------------------
dens <- rddensity(X = dt$x, c = 0)
summary(dens)
plot(dens)

# ---- 4. Main RD estimate (bias‐corrected local polynomial) ------
# Sharp RD example (outcome = y, treatment is deterministic)
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome, x = dt$x, p = 2, h = NULL) # IK h by default
summary(rd_out)   # includes robust bias‐corrected CI

# ---- 5. Fuzzy RD example ----------------------------------------
rd_fuzzy <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome, x = dt$x, fuzzy = dt$treat, p = 2)
summary(rd_fuzzy)

# ---- 6. Kink design (RKD) ---------------------------------------
# rdrobust implements RKD via specification of derivative=TRUE
rkd_out <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome, x = dt$x, deriv = 1, p = 3)
summary(rkd_out)

# ---- 7. Robustness check: bandwidth sensitivity -----------------
bw_seq <- seq(0.05, 0.5, by = 0.05)
estimates <- lapply(bw_seq, function(h){
  est <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome, x = dt$x, p = 2, h = h)
  data.table(h = h,
             point = est$Estimate[1,1],
             se_bc = est$se[1],
             ci_l = est$ci[1,1],
             ci_u = est$ci[1,2])
})
estimates <- rbindlist(estimates)
plot(estimates$h, estimates$point, type="b",
     ylim = range(c(estimates$ci_l, estimates$ci_u)),
     ylab = "Treatment effect", xlab = "Bandwidth (h)")
arrows(estimates$h, estimates$ci_l, estimates$h, estimates$ci_u, length = 0)

# ---- 8. Cluster‐robust re-estimation ----------------------------
rd_cluster <- rdrobust(y = dt$outcome, x = dt$x,
                       cluster = dt$village, p = 2)
summary(rd_cluster)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Simulation: By construction the true average treatment effect at the cutoff is known; the proposed RBC and “honest” intervals should achieve ≈95 % empirical coverage for nominal 95 % CIs even when the researcher selects aggressive (larger) bandwidths.

Empirical illustration (Progresa): Previous studies find positive impacts of cash transfers on school attendance and food consumption. I therefore expect a positive discontinuity at the poverty score cutoff—roughly 5–10 percentage-point increase in school attendance for children near the eligibility threshold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Sharp RD example)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Smooth density of running variable at cutoff ………………… 1  
C2: Covariates smooth at cutoff (balance tests) ………………… 1  
C3: Correctly specified local polynomial & robust bandwidth …… 1  
C4: No spillovers or interference around cutoff ………………… 0.5  
C5: Sufficient observations close to cutoff for precision ……… 1  

Total ≈ 4.5 / 5.  
I view the design as highly credible subject to empirical confirmation of density and covariate balance tests and the absence of cross-unit spillovers.
